title: Ignatius to the Romans
subtitle: a condemned bishop begs a church not to save him
lead: A prisoner on his way to die writes ahead to the church in the city of his death. Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, has been condemned to the wild beasts and is being taken to Rome under a guard of ten soldiers. At Smyrna he hears that the Roman Christians may try to have him freed. This letter asks them, with all the force he has, to do nothing: 'I am God's wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts so that I may be found pure bread of Christ' (4:1).

It is the one letter of his that is not written to thank its readers, and Irenaeus, Eusebius and Jerome all quote it. It opens with a greeting the churches read in different ways, to the church that 'presides in the region of the Romans' and is 'presiding over the love' (1:0). No church counts it as Scripture. It is read here as a witness to the faith of the generation after the apostles, with the New Testament as the measure.
facts: No church. It is not in the New Testament of the Council of Trent (Catholic), the Westminster Confession (Reformed), the Second London Baptist Confession, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's list of 35 New Testament books, or the Thirty-Nine Articles' 'Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received'. Ignatius himself sets his words below the apostles' (4:3).

Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria ('the overseer of Syria', 2:2). Eusebius names the letter among the seven he wrote on his way to Rome (Church History 3.36.6), and Irenaeus quotes it about AD 180 (Against Heresies 5.28.4).

Dated in its last verse 'the ninth day before the Kalends of September', which Lake renders 24 August (10:3); no year is given. Eusebius's Chronicle puts the martyrdom 'in the tenth year of Trajan, i.e. 108 A.D.' (as Lake reports it); Jerome, 'the eleventh year of Trajan' (Lives of Illustrious Men 16). Lake: 'there is a general tendency to think that Ignatius was really a martyr in Rome in the time of Trajan (98-117 A.D.)'.
Smyrna, in Asia (10:1), with delegates from Ephesus beside him
The church at Rome, before Ignatius arrived

Kirsopp Lake's Greek (Loeb, 1912), the short (middle) recension. Romans came down apart from the other six letters, in a tenth-century Paris manuscript that holds it inside an account of Ignatius's martyrdom (published by Ruinart in 1689), and in the Latin, Armenian and Syriac versions and the long recension.
authorship: The letter claims to be by 'Ignatius, also called Theophorus', 'the overseer of Syria', writing from Smyrna on the way to his death in Rome (1:0; 2:2; 10:1). Eusebius knew seven letters of his and quotes this one (Church History 3.36.6-9); Irenaeus quotes 4:1 as the words of 'a certain man of ours ... condemned to the wild beasts' (Against Heresies 5.28.4); Polycarp, who knew him, collected his letters (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2). The Catholic Encyclopedia says that with Irenaeus's quotation 'the evidence of authenticity becomes compelling'.

Three forms of the letters survive (Lake): a long recension of thirteen letters with interpolations, the short recension of the seven Eusebius names, and a Syriac abridgment of three (Ephesians, Romans and Polycarp) that Cureton published in 1845 and for a time thought original. The Catholic Encyclopedia describes how Calvin rejected the letters, how 'the reformer Dallaeus', at Geneva in 1666, questioned all seven and the Anglican Pearson defended them in 1672,. In 1910 the Catholic Encyclopedia wrote: 'While it can hardly be said that there is at present any unanimous agreement on the subject, the best modern criticism favors the authenticity of the seven letters mentioned by Eusebius', naming Zahn, Lightfoot and Harnack. Later in the twentieth century the question was opened again. Sergio Zañartu's survey of the recent discussion (Teología y Vida, 2009) names R. Weijenborg (1969), who argued that the short recension was made from the long one; R. Joly (1979), who held the letters a forgery written in Smyrna between 165 and 168; J. Rius-Camps (1980), who kept as genuine only the four letters written from Smyrna; R. M. Hübner (1997), who dated the letters between 165 and 175; and his student T. Lechner (1999). Zañartu quotes W. R. Schoedel (1987), who expected the short recension to remain what 'the scholarly consensus today' sees in it, 'a collection of genuine letters of Bishop Ignatius of Antioch', and C. Munier's survey of a century of research (1993), which found no reason in 'the general opinion of historians and patrologists' to give up the conclusions of the nineteenth-century scholars. Zañartu himself, after weighing the objections, holds to the short recension's authenticity 'until the contrary is proved' (the quotations from his survey are the site's translations). On the other side, B. A. Zuiddam (Ekklesiastikos Pharos, 2010) argues that the seven-letter text may be a medieval abridgment, and that either the whole collection is 'a pious fraud to strengthen orthodoxy of a later date' or eleven letters are Ignatius's own. Lake follows the short recension.

audience.to: The church at Rome, which Ignatius had never seen. The letter assumes that it had members with the standing or means to get a condemned man freed ('it is easy for you to do what you want', 1:2; 'if you keep silent', 2:1; 'do not become an untimely kindness to me', 4:1), that Peter and Paul had once taught it (4:3), and that it had taught other churches (3:1). Some Christians from Syria had gone ahead of Ignatius and were already in Rome (10:2).
audience.why: Lake: 'The "Romans" has the object of preventing the Christians at Rome from making any efforts to save Ignatius from the beasts in the arena, and so robbing him of the crown of martyrdom.' It is the only one of his letters not written to thank its readers. Knowing this explains its strange shape: the praise of the greeting, the plea not to act, the pictures of death as birth and of the beasts as millstones are all aimed at stopping a rescue.

outline: Greeting to the church that presides in the region of the Romans
His hope to see them, and his fear that their love will save him
To be found a Christian, not only called one
God's wheat; not as Peter and Paul
Ten leopards; now I am beginning to be a disciple
My birth is upon me; let me imitate my God's suffering
The ruler of this age; living water; God's bread
Pray for the church in Syria

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Reads the letter as a source: the journey under guard, Ignatius's death in Rome and its date, the separate history of the text (Ruinart's manuscript, the versions), the dated last line, and the ancient writers who quoted it.

lenses.name: New Testament
lenses.desc: Follows the New Testament in the letter: Paul above all (1 Corinthians in Lake's margin at 4:3, 5:1, 6:1 and 9:2; Peter and Paul as apostles, 4:3), and John (living water, God's bread, David's seed in chapter 7), and what Ignatius does with their words.

lenses.name: Church and churches
lenses.desc: Reads the letter for the questions churches still ask of it: the Roman church that 'presides' (1:0), the seeking and refusing of rescue in martyrdom, and 'God's bread ... the flesh of Jesus Christ' (7:3).

sections.b: Every other letter of Ignatius thanks a church for its kindness and warns it against division or false teaching. This one warns against nothing but love. The Romans can save him; he asks them not to (1:2; 2:1; 4:1). The whole letter is built to that end: he praises them (1:0; 3:1), tells them what his death means to him (4:1-2; 6:1-2), shows he is already suffering (5:1-3), and warns that the devil would use their kindness (7:1). He even asks them not to listen to him if he begs for his life in person (7:2).

sections.h: The Roman church in the greeting
sections.b: The greeting calls the Roman church the one that 'presides in the region of the Romans' and is 'presiding over the love' (1:0). Catholic teaching cites it for the Roman church that 'presides in charity' (Catechism 834; Lumen Gentium 13); the Orthodox theologian Thomas Hopko reads a place of honor and 'presidency in love'; the Anglican scholar Lightfoot says the presidency is the church's, not its bishop's, and that 'the idea of the "cathedra Petri" therefore has no place here'. The letter itself never mentions a bishop of Rome. See the notes at 1:0; the question of Peter's successors is on the card at Matthew 16:18.

Ignatius became 'food for wild beasts', as Eusebius puts it (Church History 3.36.3), in the shows in which criminals were killed by animals in the amphitheater. He turns the arena into a mill and an altar: the beasts' teeth grind him into bread (4:1), and his blood is poured out like wine (2:2). He calls his guards 'leopards' and his journey a fight with beasts (5:1), and lists the deaths he may suffer without flinching (5:3). On the shows see the topic 'Gladiators, Races and Shows'.

The Greek manuscript at Florence that preserves the other six letters of the short recension 'omits the epistle to the Romans' (Lake). 'This deficiency was supplied in 1689 by Ruinart in his Acta Martyrum Sincera from a Paris MS. (Paris Graec. 1451) of the 10th century.' The Catholic Encyclopedia explains that the Paris manuscript (it calls it the Codex Colbertinus) holds Romans inside an account of the martyrdom, the 'Martyrium Colbertinum'. Lake's footnotes still call the Greek 'G', though his list of symbols gives G as the Florence manuscript only. Lightfoot's list explains the use: 'G. Greek Original (Medicean and Colbertine mss)', and for this letter the Colbertine, the Paris manuscript, is 'the only extant Greek ms which contains this epistle'. So in Romans 'G' is the Paris manuscript. Besides it there are the Latin version Robert Grosseteste made in 1250, the Armenian, the Syriac (with Cureton's abridgment, which includes Romans), the long recension, and the ancient quotations. Lake judges the text of the letters 'fairly accurate, though it is probably by no means so good as that of I. Clement'.

Irenaeus quotes 4:1 (Against Heresies 5.28.4, in the Greek Eusebius preserves). Eusebius quotes 5:1-3, introducing it as 'word for word' though his text differs in small ways (see the variant at 5:3), and then Irenaeus's quotation (Church History 3.36.7-12). Jerome gives a Latin form of chapter 5 and 4:1 in his life of Ignatius (Lives of Illustrious Men 16). Origen quoted 'my love is crucified' (7:2), as Lightfoot reports. The Orthodox Church in America's life of the saint quotes 6:1 and 7:2.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a letter written to be read aloud in the arena's city
spec.body: The letter is full of public pictures: a choir round an altar (2:2), a sunset seen from the east (2:2), a mill (4:1), a tomb (4:2), a freed slave (4:3). Ignatius also asks the Romans to believe his letter over his own voice if he weakens (7:2). I suggest he wrote it to be read to the whole Roman church before he arrived, so that the church as a body, not only a few powerful members, would commit itself not to intervene. This is my reading; Lake and Lightfoot say only that the letter aims to stop a rescue.

canon.summary: Ignatius to the Romans is an early Christian letter in no church's Bible. Its author, the martyr Ignatius of Antioch, is commemorated in the calendars of the Catholic Church in the United States, the Orthodox Church in America and the Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod.
accepted_by: Not Scripture: the Council of Trent's list of New Testament books (1546) does not include it. The U.S. bishops' liturgical calendar keeps 17 October as the Memorial of 'Saint Ignatius of Antioch, Bishop and Martyr'. The Catechism quotes this letter's greeting for the Roman church 'which presides in charity' (Catechism 834).
The Orthodox Church in America commemorates 'Hieromartyr Ignatius the God-Bearer, Bishop of Antioch' on 20 December, and its life of him quotes this letter.
Not Scripture: the church's list of 35 New Testament books, which adds eight books to the 27, among them 'The book of Clement' and the 'Didascalia', does not name it.
Not Scripture: Article VI receives 'All the Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received'.
The synod's Southern District page for the commemoration of 'Ignatius of Antioch, Pastor and Martyr' (17 October) says he was 'thrown to the wild beasts in the arena' and names the seven letters.
Not Scripture: the Westminster Confession lists the 27 books of the New Testament as 'all the books of the Old and New Testaments, which are these'.
Not Scripture: the Second London Baptist Confession (1689) lists the same 27 books, 'All of which are given by the inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life'.

provenance.h: Smyrna, on the road to Rome
provenance.b: Ignatius wrote from Smyrna (10:1), where, Eusebius says, he also wrote to Ephesus, Magnesia and Tralles, before going on to Troas (Church History 3.36.5-6, 10). He was under military guard (5:1) and had been condemned to the beasts. The letter is dated 24 August, in Lake's rendering (10:3).

Unlike the other six letters, Romans is missing from the Florence manuscript of the short recension and was printed from a tenth-century Paris manuscript in 1689 by Ruinart (Lake). The Catholic Encyclopedia says that manuscript holds Romans 'associated with the "Martyrium Colbertinum"', an account of Ignatius's martyrdom. The letter is also in Grosseteste's Latin, the Armenian, the Syriac and Cureton's Syriac abridgment, and the long recension.

rejected_why.h: It does not claim apostolic authority
rejected_why.b: The early church received into the New Testament writings it held to come from the apostles and their circle. Ignatius sets himself apart from them: 'I am not commanding you as Peter and Paul did. They were apostles; I am a condemned man' (4:3). He calls himself 'the last' of his own church and 'one born at the wrong time' (9:2), borrowing Paul's words for himself.

rejected_why.h: Treated as a bishop's letter, not a book of the canon
rejected_why.b: Eusebius tells the story of Ignatius and quotes this letter in his history (Church History 3.36), but he does not mention Ignatius in his survey of the books accepted, disputed and rejected for the New Testament (Church History 3.25). Jerome lists the seven letters in his lives of church writers (Lives of Illustrious Men 16), as he lists other bishops' writings.

cited_in.b: Paul's letter to the same church praised its faith as known 'in the whole world'. Ignatius praises it as a church that has 'taught others' (3:1).
Ignatius takes Paul's words 'one born at the wrong time' and 'the least' for himself (Lake's margin). The direction is from Paul to Ignatius: the New Testament does not quote this letter.
Paul's picture of himself 'poured out as a drink offering' is behind Ignatius's verb in 2:2, a verb of the same family (also 2 Timothy 4:6).
'God's bread' is the phrase of John 6:33, in Lake's margin; with John 4:10 and 7:38 (living water) it shows Ignatius's use of John's language.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to what Christians believed in the generation after the apostles the letter is of the first importance: it is early (Lake reports a general tendency to date Ignatius's death under Trajan, 98-117), its author was a leader of the church at Antioch, and it was quoted within about seventy years by Irenaeus. As a text it is good but has its own history, resting on one Paris manuscript of the tenth century, the versions and the long recension. Its few historical claims (a journey under guard from Syria through Smyrna to Rome, a condemnation to the beasts) fit what Eusebius reports. Its teaching mostly follows Paul and John, and goes beyond them in its eagerness for death.

sections.h: 1. As a witness to early Christian belief
sections.b: High. The letter shows a church leader who calls Jesus Christ 'our God' (1:0), speaks of 'the suffering of my God' (6:3), knows Peter and Paul as the apostles who taught Rome (4:3), uses Paul's and John's language, and calls the faith 'Christianity' (3:3). It shows the Roman church already honored in the East (1:0) and the churches of Asia sending delegates to a prisoner (9:3; 10:1).

Good, with gaps in certainty. Lake judges the text of the seven letters 'fairly accurate, though it is probably by no means so good as that of I. Clement'. Romans rests on a different Greek manuscript from the others, the versions and the ancient quotations. Several readings are uncertain: 'named after Christ' or 'keeping Christ's law' (1:0), 'good' or 'eternal' (3:3), 'pure bread of Christ' or 'of God' (4:1), 'unwilling' or 'willing' (5:2), 'speaking' or 'leaping' water (7:2). See the variants.

The letter claims to be written by Ignatius at Smyrna on 24 August, on the way to Rome under guard (1:1; 5:1; 10:1-3). Eusebius knew it as his, writes that he 'became food for wild beasts' ('the story is', in his words), and quotes it (Church History 3.36.3-9). The genuineness of the seven letters was disputed from the 1600s to the 1800s (the Catholic Encyclopedia names Dallaeus, Pearson and Cureton), and it was renewed in the twentieth century: the authorship section gives the Catholic Encyclopedia's judgment of 1910, with its caveat, and the later challenges and replies. Whether the Romans did try to free him, and how he died, the letter cannot say.

Matches: Christ's death and rising 'for us' (6:1; Romans 4:25), the Spirit as living water (7:2; John 7:38-39), Christ of David's line (7:3; Romans 1:3), the world's hatred of the faithful (3:3; John 15:19), imitation of Christ (6:3; 1 Corinthians 11:1). Goes beyond: its longing for death and its plea against rescue go further than Paul, who longed 'to leave and be with Christ' but chose to stay for the churches (Philippians 1:23-25); a generation later the Martyrdom of Polycarp said 'we give no praise to people who turn themselves in' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 4:1). Its titles for the Roman church (1:0) have no parallel in the New Testament. Conflicts: none on a point of doctrine; the letter does not take up Jesus's word to escape from one town to the next (Matthew 10:23).

how_to_read.h: As a letter, not a treatise
how_to_read.b: Ignatius writes fast, under strain, in a crowded and broken Greek. Read it whole, as one plea, and let the pictures (wheat, altar, sunset, birth) carry the argument.

how_to_read.h: With the New Testament beside it
how_to_read.b: Most of its strongest lines rework Paul and John. Read the passages in the notes (1 Corinthians 15:8; Philippians 2:17; John 4:10; John 6:33) to see what Ignatius borrows and what he adds.

how_to_read.h: As a witness, not a rule
how_to_read.b: No church reads it as Scripture. Churches that honor Ignatius as a saint read it as the testimony of a martyr; on the questions it raises (Rome's place, seeking martyrdom, the Supper) the notes give the readings of the churches from their own sources and point to the cards on the 66 books.
